chunks: Ibrahim ibn Hashim from Abd al-Rahman ibn Hammad al-Kufi from Ibrahim ibn Abd al-Hamid from Isa said:

"Whoever stays the night intending to fast the next day, that intention binds him; if he breaks the fast, he must make up for it. And whoever wakes up and did not intend to fast from the night, he has the choice until the sun sets; if he wishes, he fasts, and if he wishes, he breaks the fast. If the sun sets and he has not eaten, he should complete the fast until night."

Therefore, this report is understood as referring to a type of preference (istihbab), because the earlier reports indicate that he may break the fast at any time he wishes without making it up, and it is possible that this is specific to making up the fast of Ramadan, for if he breaks the fast in it after midday, he is obligated to make it up along with expiation, as we will explain later, if God Almighty wills.
ai.seo_question: What are the Shia rulings on fasting intention and breaking the fast during the day?
ai.summary: This narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* establishes the foundational Shia juristic distinction between *niyyah* (intention) made during the night versus the day, granting those who slept without intention the flexibility to choose until solar noon (*zawal*). The commentary highlights a critical scholarly nuance: while breaking the fast without prior intention is generally permissible without penalty, this ruling is likely specific to voluntary fasts, whereas in Ramadan, breaking the fast after *zawal* incurs both *qada'* (making up the day) and *kaffarah* (expiation). This reflects the broader Shia principle that intention is a condition for the validity of worship, yet the timing of that intention determines the severity of the consequence for breaking it.
